tagline.text: A mountain reserve in central Mindoro, home of the endangered tamaraw

location.label: Location
location.text: South-central Mindoro, around Sablayan and Calintaan in Occidental Mindoro (extending into Oriental Mindoro)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~6,000 (per person, 3 days 2 nights from Manila, group arrangement)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: San Jose Airport (SJI), or overland and by boat from Manila

children.text: Mounts Iglit-Baco Natural Park is a protected area of about 106,000 hectares in south-central Mindoro. It is the last habitat of the tamaraw, an endangered small wild buffalo found only on this island, and is dominated by Mount Iglit (about 1,432 m) and Mount Baco (2,488 m).

Mounts Iglit-Baco Natural Park is a protected area in south-central Mindoro. It spans Sablayan, Calintaan, Rizal and San Jose in Occidental Mindoro and Bongabong, Bansud, Gloria and Mansalay in Oriental Mindoro, and Sablayan holds about 68 percent of the area. On June 22, 2018, Republic Act 11038 changed its status from national park to natural park and enlarged it from 75,445 hectares to about 106,655 hectares. It began in 1969 as a game refuge and bird sanctuary, became a national park on November 9, 1970, and was designated an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2003. The park is managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), and the protected area office is in Sitio Tamisan, Poypoy, Calintaan. Only 322 visitors were recorded from November 2019 to February 2020, so it is far quieter than ordinary tourist spots.

The star of the park is the tamaraw. The tamaraw (Bubalus mindorensis) is a small wild buffalo found only on Mindoro and is critically endangered. The population, estimated at about 10,000 in the early 1990s according to one source, is now thought to be under 600, and the April 2018 count found 523, up from 327 in 2012. More than 80 percent of them live in a single area of about 2,500 hectares. The park also has 25 endemic species (including 7 birds, 9 mammals and 3 amphibians), as well as Philippine deer and wild pigs. Breeding of tamaraws has continued since 1979 at the Tamaraw Gene Pool Farm, and a conservation program still counts the animals.

The mountains have two main peaks. Mount Baco in the north is the highest at 2,488 m, and Wikipedia gives Mount Iglit in the south as about 2,364 m. But Philippine mountaineering guides and trek reports give about 1,432 m, so the heights differ greatly and it is safest not to state one flatly. Grassland, lowland dipterocarp forest and montane rainforest follow one another, and the most extensive remaining forest is around Mount Baco in the north. Ten major rivers run from these mountains to the Sibuyan Sea and the South China Sea.

This guide is for people who want to see the tamaraw in person or to hike deep in Mindoro. Unlike an ordinary beach trip, it needs permits, registration and a local guide, and it is a trek that includes camping and river crossings. You cannot go without a guide and there is no fixed timetable, so contact the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) or the Tamaraw Conservation Program first. Trail conditions and costs change over time, and some figures in this guide come from 2017–2018 trip reports.

The most likely place is the Tamaraw Plaza near the summit of Mount Magawang. They are said to appear at sunrise or around sunset, and are almost never seen once the heat rises. You watch from a distance through a telescope and cannot approach.

Known as a peak of about 1,432 m, it offers a 360-degree view of grassland and nearby islands from the top. It is said to take 4 to 5 hours from Camp 2 (the Tamaraw ranger station) to the summit, and reports mention rappelling at cliff sections.
A low peak that you can climb in 1 to 2 hours from Camp 2 and a tamaraw viewing point. A common plan is to climb at dusk, watch along with the sunset and then come down.

Between Camp 1 and Camp 2, over 3 to 4 hours, you cross rivers many times and pass a wooden bridge known as the Monkey Bridge. After heavy rain the water level can rise and be dangerous, so the guide decides.
The park is also the ancestral land of Mangyan groups such as the Tao Buid. Many do not speak Tagalog, so ask permission before taking photos and respect local ways.

The park has 25 endemic species, along with animals such as the Mindoro climbing rat and the Mindoro stripe-faced fruit bat. At least 25 threatened plant species are also recorded, including the rare jade vine.

Near the park in Sablayan is Apo Reef, known as the Philippines' largest coral reef, so many travelers combine mountain and sea in one trip. If you want to hike more, Mount Calavite in Paluan, Occidental Mindoro (about 1,521 m, a 1–2 day hike) is described as a climb to a summit with an old communication tower.
Travel from Manila to Batangas Port, take the night boat to Abra de Ilog and go by van to Calintaan. According to one report, you have breakfast and shop for supplies in Calintaan after arriving.
Meet your guide in Poypoy and travel by tractor.
Register at the military detachment and at Camp 1, then start walking.
Pass the wooden bridge known as the Monkey Bridge and cross the river several times before lunch. In one report the sixth river crossing came at about 12:30.
Arrive at Camp 2, have lunch and rest.
Climb Mount Magawang and watch for tamaraws from the viewing deck at dusk. Come down around 17:30, have dinner at camp and sleep at 22:00.
On the second day, set off for Mount Iglit at dawn. There is rappelling at cliff sections, and you cross the ridge around 7:00 and reach the summit.
Descend, have lunch at Camp 2 and return through Camp 1 to the village in the afternoon.
This schedule is based on one 2017 group-trip report. Follow your guide and DENR instructions for the actual plan.
Walk from Camp 1 up to Camp 2 and stay overnight.
Watch for tamaraws from Mount Magawang at dawn, then descend.
Plan the itinerary with your guide according to your fitness and the weather.
There are flights from Manila to San Jose Airport (SJI), with a flight time of about
1 hour
. Airlines and whether flights operate change with the season, so check when booking.
From San Jose town, take a tricycle to the Tamaraw Conservation Program (TCP) office. Check the office location locally.

items.title: Overland and by boat from Manila

children.text: A bus from Manila to Batangas Port takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–3 hours
, and the boat from Batangas to Abra de Ilog takes about
2 hours 30 minutes
(2017 source, fare about ₱260).

From Abra de Ilog to Calintaan or San Jose, a van takes 3 to 4 hours and a bus takes longer. Direct buses (including the boat) are said to exist, but fares and times come from old sources, so they need checking.
The entrance is Poypoy village in Calintaan. Show your permit at the barangay hall and go by tricycle or tractor to Camp 1 (Magtangcob village). On foot it takes about
1 hour
Register at the military detachment in front of Camp 1, then walk with your guide.
For permits, you pay the trekking fee and the DENR environmental fee at the TCP office, and pay an entrance fee separately at the barangay hall. Items may change, so check on site.

You cross rivers many times and there is almost no shade on the grassland, so the dry season, December–May, is best. Even in the dry season it is hot and humid by day, so it is better to start early in the morning.
In the rainy season, June–November, rivers swell and are hard to cross, and the paths are slippery and dangerous. The guide may not allow entry at that time.

Tamaraw watching is best in the early morning and around dusk, and on cloudy days they are said to stay visible longer. In the midday heat they hide in the forest and are almost never seen, so do not expect to see them around noon.

Inside the park you sleep at Camp 2 (the Tamaraw ranger station), where toilets and water are available. Outside the park, beach resorts in Sablayan (such as Gustav's Place) and hotels in San Jose (such as Mindoro Plaza Hotel and Sikatuna Beach Hotel) are listed. Prices change with the season, so check locally.
Guides or camps often prepare meals, and you can buy snacks and water at the markets in San Jose and Calintaan. The rule is to carry your trash out.

Pack a waterproof bag, dry spare clothes, sun protection, a headlamp, trash bags and a personal first-aid kit. Camps have toilets and water, but it is safer to bring plenty of drinking water of your own. From the top of Mount Iglit you see grassland and nearby islands in 360 degrees, and since starts are early, it is best to go to bed early in the evening.
Permits are said to be issued at the TCP office, but the required documents may change. Contact the DENR first.
Start at dawn to avoid the daytime heat. There is almost no shade above Camp 2.
Water is said to be available partway along the route to the Iglit summit and at Magawang camp. Bring purification tablets and a large water bottle.
Tamaraws are best seen at sunrise and sunset. Binoculars or a zoom lens help.
You must cross rivers, so bring a waterproof bag and spare socks.
If you meet Mangyan people, ask permission before taking photos.
Follow the Leave No Trace principles.
The park is a protected area that you cannot enter without a guide and a permit. In the rainy season, swollen rivers can block entry.
Do not approach or feed tamaraws. Watch them only from a distance.
The fare and transport information here includes 2017–2018 sources. Be sure to recheck before you leave.
There are cliff sections and river crossings, so beginners and people with low fitness should choose an easier itinerary.
Mobile signal and access to hospitals are difficult inside the park. Agree on first-aid supplies and an emergency contact method with your guide beforehand.
A coral reef off Sablayan known as the largest in the Philippines, good to combine with the mountains for a trip that joins the mountains and the sea.
A beach resort in northern Mindoro that you can stop at for rest after the trek.
A port city from which boats leave from Manila to Mindoro.
The main city of Occidental Mindoro near the park, with an airport and hotels.
